Conceptualization

Conceptualization involves creating game concepts and turning them into conceptual designs.

Creative Process

  • The creative process can be one of the hardest parts of conceptualizing a game idea.
  • Creativity has no one-size-fits-all solution - however, there are some steps that can be carried out to streamline the process.

Preparation
Preparation is all about creating a stimulating environment/space where creativity can flow.

Incubation
Once the environment is sufficient for creativity, incubation is about getting into the correct headspace to allow the formulation of new ideas.

Insight
Refers to the moment when an idea gets formulated. Once this has taken place the idea can be evaluated

Evaluation
Evaluation refers to an analysis of a formulated idea and can mean asking questions such as how effective an idea is and whether it is worth continuing to develop it.

Elaboration
It is often considered better to refine an idea as opposed to throwing 'bad' ideas out. Elaborating could involve combining and developing multiple 'bad' ideas into a good idea.

Crafting Ideas

Numerous ways of working exist when it comes to the idea initiation process. Crafting processes may be effective for some people but less effective for others.

  • Brainstorming: Discuss various ideas in a group setting and decide which ideas resonate and which do not.
  • List Creation: Create a list of various ideas.
  • Idea Cards: Various ideas put on cards which are shuffled and selected.
  • Mind Maps
  • Stream of Consciousness: Talk non-stop about various ideas or just keep writing ideas - keeping nothing off limits
  • Shout It Out: Can stimulate further thinking
  • Cut It Up: Combination of various ideas
  • Research: Academic publications, YouTube videos, etc.

Elevator Pitch: A short summary that can be used to quickly and simply define a game concept, as if you are explaining it to someone in an elevator. Has to be catchy and enthusiastic

Idea Refinement

Once ideas are formulated, they can be refined to match the feasibility of the tools available.

Technical Feasibility: Refers to the technical aspects of implementing the game idea presented.

  • Will it be possible with the game engine provided?
  • Will it work for the end user's technology?
  • Does the game platform make use of controls that work for the idea given?

Market Opportunity: Refers to research into the potential game audience, such as how popular the game will be and whether it will be successful.

Artistic Considerations: Refers to developing an idea so that both the audience and developer will like what has been created. Artistic elements have to match the expectations of the player.

  • For example, art of a more professional nature will be needed for games that are designed professionally and sold at a more premium price.

Business/Cost Restrictions: Refers to budgeting and time constraints. Will the game/idea be ready by the release time?

Moving From Concept to Design

Once a game and elevator pitch have been constructed and the concept is complete, the process of designing the game can begin.

Formal Element Focus
The formal elements are a large area of focus in design.

Game Structure

  • Flowcharts are an architectural diagram type that can be used to map out procedures, such as in turn-based games.

Interaction & Planning Design Choice

  • Interaction: Will the game make use of a high amount of player-to-player interaction (e.g. Chess), or a low amount of player-to-player interaction? (e.g. Bingo)
  • Planning: Will the game make use of long-term planning (e.g. Chess) or short-term planning? (e.g. Bingo)

The Game Design Process

Design Phases

  • The game design process will consist of numerous design phases, which will eventually interlink to form a fully functional, playable game.
  • These phases include designs for the system, levels, content, interfaces, world, and narratives.

System Design
How are the underlying game systems designed (e.g. scores)

Level Design
How will different levels be designed and what distinguishes them?

Content Design
How will the content be designed on a technical level?

Interface Design
How does the user interact with your game?

World Design
How do you fit lore/background detailing into your game?

Narrative Design
How are the game story/story arcs built together?

Design Approaches

Every game will benefit from different design strategies and every person will work better with different strategies.

  • Blue-Sky Design: No limits, no judgement.
  • Slow-Boil Storylines: Slow process-driven narrative where storyline emerges from trivial situations
  • Mechanic-Driven: Mechanics such as turns or collection of objects become a key theme in the design process.
  • Intellectual Property: Game is based on a known franchise or brand e.g. Pokémon, Mario
  • Story-Centered: Design approach where a storyline already exists and the game is built around it.
  • Research-Driven: Concept design is driven from research done into the game's area of focus.
  • Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics Design: A layered approach where the design of the game mechanics will influence the dynamics (interactions), which then influence the visuals. Players, unlike developers, will see the aesthetics/visuals first.
  • Game Rules/ScEnario Model (GREM): A time-based approach where the proportions of time spent on each element are worked out in advance.
    • GREM can be done in a modular way i.e. common/shared mechanisms can be used.
    • A GREM Engine exists and allows for the creation of low-level game mechanics (it won't create sprites)

UML is a useful tool for mapping out game interactions and represent implementation aspects, such as through activity diagrams.

However, due to UML's low-level modelling focus, it is deemed unsuitable for diagramming high-level/user-level architectures.

High level architecture diagrams do not need to be as in-depth or specific as typically specified by UML's design rules.

This allows for a large amount of insight to be provided in a relatively straightforward diagram.

Prototyping

  • Prototyping involves creating a small part of element of a game and testing it out to determine its effectiveness.
  • Prototypes can be physical or digital and will highlight various formal elements of interest.
  • Rules will be added to turn the prototype into a functional game
  • Refinement is then undertaken on the prototype in order to produce the full game or next prototype.

Physical Prototyping

  • Physical prototyping is cheap and quick and is often carried out, specifically for board games.
  • They focus on gameplay as opposed to technology.
    • It can be hard to depict technical elements e.g. framerates on a physical prototype.
  • Physical prototypes allow for real time response feedback from players, especially if the players have no technical experience.
  • A low cost also allows for broader experimentation processes with physical prototyping.

Digital Prototyping: 4 Types

Game Mechanics: Prototypes of various aspects of gameplay such as movement or character interactions.

Aesthetics: Prototypes of visual/audial elements such as sprite designs, fonts, background music, etc.

Kinesthetics: Prototypes of movement and controls, such as player jump patterns. This cannot be done physically.

Technology: Prototypes of game technologies such as enemy AI or game physics.

  • Digital Prototyping is often done in another programming language since they need to be cheap, quick and disposable.
  • Doing them in the same language would often result in too much time being spent on prototyping, which can interfere with budget/time constraints.

Prototyping Rules of Thumb

  • A question should always be asked in order to form a hypothesis and/or purpose.
  • Prototypes should stay falsifiable e.g. they should be thrown out in the event that they do not work as intended.
  • Prototypes should be fun, persuade, and inspire the testers.
  • Prototypes need to minimize 'time to first failure' i.e. they should be fast.
  • Prototypes must be economical to the budget
  • They must be very limited in scope.

Playtesting

  • The game design process is an iterative process involving continual refinement, testing, evaluating and new prototyping.
  • Throughout this process, playtesting can be carried out with individuals who are willing to test game prototypes.

There are various ways to conduct playtesting, each giving a variation on results.

Playtesting Methods

  • One-on-one testing
  • Group testing
  • Feedback forms
  • Interviews
  • Open discussions
  • Data hooks and/or metrics

It is important to note that game developers will have the most expertise regarding their game. This makes it important to gain different perspectives through testing with a target audience.

Playtesting of Specific Situations
Towards the end of testing stages, it may be more useful to examine specific game stages in testing, e.g. the end of the game, random spawn events.
